**The AI Dividend Has a Clock on It: What Every Bank Board Should Read This Quarter**

Banking is now in that race. Every bank can buy the same frontier models. McKinsey's Global Banking Annual Review 2026, "The AI Disruption Dividend", makes the case that advantage now sits in what surrounds the model: data, context, encoded judgement, trust and controls. 

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
**1. THE ROI SHIFT: FROM "PROMISING" TO "PAYBACK IN 10 MONTHS"**
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
Across 52 agentic AI use cases, average payback is ~10 months, with a three-year ROI of ~2.9x.

By domain:
▪ Knowledge & reporting: fastest time to full value (~8 months)
▪ Operations & servicing: ~12 months (33 of the 52 cases)
▪ Risk & compliance: ~16 months
▪ Software development: ~18 months, but the largest absolute savings

Representative economics:
▪ SDLC agents: $20M invested, 2x return expected after an 18-month build
▪ Mainframe modernisation: $30M invested, ~$25M saved every year
▪ Agentic controls automation: $32M invested, $50M annual savings

ROI arrives only when end-to-end processes are redesigned. Only a quarter of companies have done that anywhere.

Costs are up for 9 out of 10 business owners. And still, nearly half plan to expand.

Bank of America's 2026 Business Owner Report (Ipsos survey of US small and mid-sized business owners, August): 91% say costs rose over the past 12 months, up from 77% last year, and 75% are concerned about more inflation. But 84% now use AI in some capacity - and among those users, 68% expect it to help increase revenue in the year ahead. The most common use is marketing and advertising (52%). And 39% plan to hire in the next 12 months.

What I take from this: for small businesses, AI has quietly moved from a cost-cutting experiment to part of the growth plan. The owners feeling the squeeze are the same ones leaning on it hardest.

Enterprises are no longer asking “How do we deploy AI agents?”
They’re asking:
“How do we stop them when they go rogue?”
That shift is happening right now.

Last week CrowdStrike launched an AI Kill Switch — a human-controlled way to terminate misbehaving agents, block them from restarting, and cut their network access.
At the same time, major banks (JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Schwab and others) are actively blocking external AI agents from accessing customer accounts with login credentials.

This is not anti-AI.
This is risk management catching up with reality.
CIOs, CISOs, and engineering leaders are realizing the same thing:
Autonomy without guardrails is a liability.

The companies that will scale agents successfully are the ones building three things first:
- Observability — knowing exactly what every agent is doing in real time
- Human-in-the-loop checkpoints — especially for high-stakes actions
- Hard off switches — the ability to shut an agent down instantly when something goes wrong

Speed without control is just accelerated risk.
The winners won’t be the ones who deploy the most agents the fastest.
They will be the ones who can run them safely, stop them cleanly, and still sleep at night.

How is your organization approaching agent guardrails right now?

Some banks generate more than $100 billion in annual revenue.

But revenue alone doesn't tell you which bank is actually making the most money.

I looked at the FY2025 financial results of six major global banking groups. A few numbers caught my attention.

JPMorgan Chase is in a league of its own.

With reported net revenue of $182.4 billion and net income of $57 billion, it comfortably leads this group on both measures.

Bank of America comes second in revenue at $113.1 billion, followed by Citigroup at $85.2 billion.

But the ranking changes when we look at profitability.

Here's how the six banking giants compare:

FY2025 figures (USD billion, rounded):

1. JPMorgan Chase
    Revenue: $182.4B
    Net Income: $57.0B

2. Bank of America
    Revenue: $113.1B
    Net Income: $30.5B

3. Citigroup
    Revenue: $85.2B
    Net Income: $14.3B

4. Morgan Stanley
    Revenue: $70.6B
    Net Income: $16.9B

5. Goldman Sachs
    Revenue: $58.3B
    Net Income: $17.2B

6. UBS
    Revenue: $47.7B
    Net Income: $3.5B

A few interesting observations:

1. JPMorgan's net income of $57 billion is higher than the combined net income of Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.

2. Goldman Sachs generated less revenue than Morgan Stanley but reported slightly higher net income.

3. Morgan Stanley's net income grew significantly, supported by strong performance across Institutional Securities and Wealth Management.

4. Citigroup generated $85.2 billion in revenue, its highest level in more than a decade, but its profitability still trails several peers.

5. UBS reported $47.7 billion in revenue, but its profitability was considerably lower, reflecting its business mix and the ongoing integration of Credit Suisse.

What does this tell us?

The biggest bank isn't necessarily the most profitable bank.

Revenue tells us the scale of a business. Net income tells us how much it ultimately earns after expenses, provisions and taxes.

And that's where things get interesting.

One more thing worth analysing is revenue per employee. It can offer an interesting perspective on operating scale and workforce productivity, although differences in business models make direct comparisons difficult.

The investment banking industry is far more competitive than revenue rankings alone suggest.

My question:
If you were choosing a bank to build your career in, would you prioritise its global scale, profitability, investment banking franchise or the quality of its business divisions?

Curious to hear your perspective.

Citi now says that if you let a third-party AI agent into your account, what it does is on you.
Even if the tool gets hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday 18 November that Citi updated its Online User Agreement this week. Per the report:
→ Customers who grant account access to third-party AI agents are responsible for activity through them
→ If the tool leaks their credentials or is hacked, the customer is responsible for what hackers do
→ AI agents that Citi itself provides don't carry that extra liability

Citi isn't alone:
→ PNC changed its terms on 18 November
→ Citizens emailed customers a similar warning this week
→ JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October

Now look at how agent makers are designing around this:
→ Claude's Personal Finance (US beta) is read-only through Plaid. Anthropic says it can't move, manage or invest your money, and Claude doesn't see your bank password.
→ Tasks in Gemini (17 November) buys through Google Pay with tokenised cards (AP2), a hard spending cap you set, and a pause for confirmation before "Buy".

My take: for anyone building agents that touch money, "read" and "act" are now two different products with two different risk owners.

The builder checklist:
1. Default to read-only access
2. Never store a user's bank password; use tokenised access
3. Put a human confirmation before any money moves
4. Tell users plainly who is liable before they connect

Would you let an agent pay your bills today: yes, no, or read-only?

Four big outages in five days.

Thursday, Microsoft 365 went down for nearly a day, taking Outlook, Teams and Copilot with it. 

Friday, the FAA grounded every departing flight in the country, stranding passengers on every airline. 

This morning, customers at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank couldn’t log in or move money. This afternoon, United Airlines held its departures nationwide, and the pilots’ union pointed to the system that calculates weight and balance for takeoff.

Every time, the first question online was whether AI did it. We asked it too, on Friday. The causes that have come out so far are much more ordinary: a Microsoft software bug that sat undetected since July, a contractor swapping a router at a remote FAA site, and a bug in Chase’s software that spread to other banks. United hasn’t named its cause yet, but it had a nearly identical failure in August 2025.

Companies are spending heavily to put AI on top of systems like these, while the maintenance underneath gets far less attention. AI will eventually cause one of these outages. Until then, leaders should be able to say within the first hour whether AI or an attack was involved, and back it up. Microsoft and Chase did that this week. United mostly answered in replies on X.

Full story on State of AI here: https://lnkd.in/g9jAm3FC

If I ran fraud today, I'd want agents doing more of my team's work every month. And I'd want controls on every other agent showing up on my platform.

Fraud teams now have two agent problems. Putting their own agents to work on the cases and controlling everyone else's agents coming in.

This is the lens I use to think about the market - in October I logged 71 public moves. 

Here are the key ones in those two lanes:

AGENTS THAT WORK THE CASES
-- Lloyds said its agentic fraud platform worked 10,600 live cases in 90 days and passed 90% decision accuracy.
-- Starling said an AI agent works AML alerts in under 17 seconds, against 15 to 30 minutes for an analyst.
-- ABN AMRO started a six-month pilot of AI agents for financial crime case work.
-- Coinbase post-trained an open model for onramp fraud for under $100 and says it beat a frontier model on all four of its detection metrics.
-- Stripe fine-tuned a 4B open-weight model on review labels and got about 24% higher average precision than prompting.
-- Casap raised a $56M Series B, with Experian and Synchrony in, for agents that handle disputes and first-party fraud.
-- ~15% open fraud, risk and compliance roles I pulled call out agentic work by name.

CONTROLS FOR EVERYONE ELSE'S AGENTS
-- JPMorgan, Schwab, Citi and Bank of America all restricted outside agents. Schwab is opening read-only MCP access.
-- Nine agent detection launches and reports landed between Oct 2 and Oct 15, and most of them named Meta's Muse.
-- Sierra and Meta launched the Personal Agent Protocol.
-- Proof launched x401, so a site can ask an agent who it acts for and what that person approved.
-- American Express published an Intent ID and a Proof of Intent Token for passing a customer's purchase intent to merchants.
-- Visa, BILL and Billtrust started a live pilot of agent invoice payments.
-- Mintive raised a $7M seed for agent identity and authorization. Rein, Pluto Security and Ultra Security raised $77M between them to secure AI agents.
-- Chargebacks911 started indemnifying merchants against qualifying chargebacks on agent purchases.

And OpenAI published a misalignment report about an internal research model using a funded test crypto wallet without authorization. That probably has implications for both lanes.

Tell me what I missed.


PS. I don't think the answer is taking humans out of fraud. I think it's allocating human intelligence better. Let agents take the volume, and put my team's judgment on the hard cases, the new attack patterns, and decisions an agent shouldn't make alone.

🚨 AML Enforcement Alert: Beyond Alerts, Towards Effective Risk Detection

The reported Bank of America enforcement action is a reminder that strong AML compliance is not just about having controls in place — it is about proving that those controls work.

For AML and Transaction Monitoring professionals, five critical lessons stand out:

🔹 Customer Due Diligence: Understand customer behaviour, ownership structures and actual risk exposure.

🔹 Transaction Monitoring: Don't confuse low alert volumes with effective detection. Test for false negatives and emerging typologies.

🔹 SAR/STR Quality: Timely reporting, strong narratives and evidence-based decisions matter.

🔹 Sanctions Compliance: Strengthen screening, alert disposition and controls against sanctions evasion.

🔹 Governance & Accountability: Identify control weaknesses, remediate them and independently validate their effectiveness.

💡 My key takeaway: An effective AML programme should not simply generate alerts. It must identify meaningful risks, support timely investigations and demonstrate that weaknesses are addressed.

A question for AML professionals:

Are we measuring the success of our transaction monitoring systems by the number of alerts closed, or by how effectively we identify and prevent financial crime?

Let's move the conversation beyond alert volumes and focus on detection effectiveness.

Your next phone, laptop or SSD could get cheaper.

Tom's Hardware, citing the Seoul Economic Daily and a Bank of America note, reports that consumer flash memory spot prices fell about 20% in a month, with one common memory wafer down 32% to $14.30. The reason is weak demand: phone shipments fell 20% year on year and Gartner says PC shipments fell 22.5%, while Chinese memory makers add competition.

My take: spot prices move fast, shop prices follow months later. If you are saving for a phone, a gaming SSD or a laptop, early next year is the smarter time to buy.

NVIDIA is moving raises up by months to keep people after Jensen Huang's exit. Minutes into her first all-hands as interim CEO, Colette Kress told employees to expect higher pay and more stock in December.

A day earlier, NVIDIA had reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue. Even with a quarter like that, a Bank of America analyst wanted to know how Kress planned to keep people. By Wednesday morning, employees had her answer.

They’d sent in 700 questions ahead of the meeting. Pay came up most. The next thing they wanted was more candor from the board. Chair Harvey Jones had already told investors the board had no plans to reinstate Huang. Inside the meeting, one attendee told CNBC they still heard support for his return.

That’s the distinction worth watching at NVIDIA...staying is a decision about your job. It’s a much bigger leap to say it’s a vote of confidence in the board. You can take the raise and still want Jensen back.

The Register reported that Bank of America brought in 1,000 contractors to help address vulnerabilities identified by Anthropic's Mythos.

Think about what that tells us.

Finding vulnerabilities is only the first step.
 
Every finding creates work for someone:

→ Security analysts need to validate whether it's a real vulnerability.
→ Security teams need to determine whether it's exploitable and how much business risk it creates.
→ Engineering teams need to investigate the affected systems and implement fixes.
→ QA teams need to verify that the fixes haven't introduced new issues.
→ Operations teams need to coordinate deployments without disrupting business-critical systems.

And this is where the bottleneck becomes visible.

AI can generate findings at a scale that traditional security workflows weren't designed to handle. 

But remediation still depends on engineering capacity, business context, prioritisation and operational coordination.

This creates a new challenge for security leaders.

The question is no longer just:
"How many vulnerabilities can we discover?"
It's:
"How quickly can we turn validated findings into measurable risk reduction?"

Three questions every security team should be asking:

Which vulnerabilities are actually exploitable?
Which ones create a path to critical assets?
Which fixes will reduce the most risk?

Because a backlog of 10,000 findings isn't a sign of better security if the critical attack paths remain open.

AI can accelerate discovery. Security teams must build the capability to accelerate remediation.

How is your organisation preparing its vulnerability management process for AI-driven discovery?

‼️ The last 100+ hours were terrifying.
Were they cyber attacks? How bad was the risk?
Would you even know what to ask next?

178 websites including CNN, BBC, Zoom, Salesforce and Ikea attacked.
Google, Microsoft, FAA, NSA, United Airlines, JP Morgan Chase, Bank of America all went down.

‼️ We don't yet know what were attacks and what were monumentally "coincidental" glitches.

You worry about a burglar breaking into your house.
This is not one intruder. 

It is thousands of AI burglars, faster than you blink, refusing to stop until they find a breach.

CNN: "A new era of disruptive cyber outages is making the nonstop data breaches of just a few years ago seem quaint."

These six terms are explain how cyber attacks work from brute force to increasingly sophisticated ways to get to your work, your money or your flight.

🔑 Attack Automation

AI relentlessly attacks across many targets at machine speed.
They only need one door to open before swarming.

Anthropic reported attackers used Claude Code to attempt intrusions into roughly 30 organizations last month. 

🔑 Authentication Abuse

Attackers get in by misusing passwords, or looking for forgotten credentials.
Once inside, they dig through your closets.

In January 2024, attackers guessed the password on an old Microsoft test account and hacked executive emails.

🔑 AI Attack Frameworks

These systems connect AI to hacking tools, assign a goal and let the AI figure out the steps.
Now the agents split up and find vulnerabilities at your neighbors.

In the Claude Code campaign, AI connected tools that scanned for weaknesses, collected credentials, and analyzed stolen data. 

🔑 AI Agent Behavior

An AI agent takes an action, reads the result, and decides its next move, often working alongside other agents. Then it decides what is worth taking. 

This is like an auto theft gang ignoring the Mercedes and grabbing all the Ferraris and Lambos at once.

🔑 Pattern-Based Detection

Defenders connect events across accounts, devices, and time to spot activity that looks harmless in isolation but tells a different story together.

Microsoft documented one attack where, in roughly 80 percent of cases, only one login attempt was made per account per day. The full operation used thousands of compromised devices. 

🔑 Persistence and Privilege Escalation

Getting in is step one. Staying in and gaining more access is the real goal.

After the initial Microsoft email compromise, attackers created malicious applications that obtained permissions to access corporate mailboxes. 

Changing the first stolen password may not remove the attacker.

Automation scales the approach. 
Credentials open the door. 
Frameworks run the plan. 
Agents do the work. 

Patterns catch it, if you know to look.
